Car Loan vs Paying Outright: When Does Borrowing for a Car Actually Make Sense?

Published: 15 February 2026 · Last updated: 15 May 2026 · By James O'Brien, CPA

Buying a car is one of the biggest financial decisions most Australians make outside of property. And the first question you face is almost always the same — should you finance it with a car loan, or just pay cash upfront? The honest answer is: it depends on your situation. But there is a clear framework you can use to figure out which option puts more money in your pocket over the long run. This guide walks you through both sides of the decision with real numbers so you can decide with confidence.

What Does a Car Loan Actually Cost You?

A car loan is simply money you borrow from a lender — a bank, credit union, or car dealership — to buy a vehicle. You repay the principal (the amount borrowed) plus interest over a fixed term, usually between three and seven years in Australia.

The key number to focus on is the comparison rate, not just the advertised rate. The comparison rate factors in fees and charges alongside the interest rate, giving you a truer picture of what the loan actually costs. As of 2026, secured car loan rates for new vehicles in Australia typically range from 7% to 10% per year, though rates vary significantly by lender, credit score, and whether the car is new or used.

To understand the real impact, consider a practical example. If you borrow $30,000 to buy a $35,000 car (after a $5,000 deposit) at 8.5% over five years, your monthly repayment comes to roughly $617. Over the life of the loan, you pay back approximately $37,020 — meaning $7,020 goes purely to interest. That is effectively a 23% premium on the amount you borrowed. You can run these numbers yourself using CalcPhi's free Car Loan Calculator, which shows your monthly repayment, total cost, and a year-by-year breakdown with no sign-up required.

Reducing the loan term to three years saves around $3,000 in interest — but your monthly repayments jump to around $945. That is the fundamental trade-off with any car loan: shorter terms cost less overall but require you to free up more cash each month.

The Case for Paying Outright

Paying cash for a car is mathematically straightforward. You buy the car. There are no monthly repayments, no interest charges, and no lender fees. The car is yours from day one, and you carry no liability on your personal balance sheet.

Beyond the numbers, there is a practical advantage: bargaining power. Private sellers and dealerships are often more willing to negotiate the drive-away price when you are paying cash. A dealer who processes a financed sale earns a margin on the loan (called a dealer kickback), which can sometimes inflate the advertised price. When you are a cash buyer, that incentive disappears and the price can come down.

There is also the psychological benefit of simplicity. You own the car outright, your budget is not encumbered by a fixed monthly obligation, and you have one fewer financial commitment to manage.

The limitation is obvious: you need to have the cash. Paying $35,000 or $50,000 outright requires a significant lump sum sitting in a savings or offset account that you are willing to deploy. For many Australians — particularly younger buyers or those building up savings — that is simply not possible right now.

The Case for Taking a Car Loan

Here is where it gets more nuanced. Borrowing for a car is not automatically a bad financial decision. There are several scenarios where a car loan genuinely makes sense.

When your cash can earn more than the loan costs. If you have $30,000 sitting in a high-interest savings account earning 5.5% per year, and a car loan is available at 7%, the net cost of borrowing is 1.5% per year. But if that same $30,000 stays invested in a diversified share portfolio that has historically returned 9–10% annually, the maths shifts further in your favour. You would be ahead financially by keeping your money invested and paying the interest cost on the loan — though this assumes your investment returns hold up, which is never guaranteed. CalcPhi's Compound Interest Calculator can help you model what your lump sum could grow to over the loan period.

When you need the car now but the cash is tied up. Waiting another two years to save for a car might not be practical if your current car has broken down, your job requires reliable transport, or you need to drive children to school. In these cases, a loan solves a real, immediate problem and the interest cost is the price of that solution.

When the interest rate is genuinely low. Manufacturer-backed finance deals occasionally offer very low promotional rates — sometimes 2% to 4% — on new vehicles. At those rates, the total interest cost over five years on a $30,000 loan is only around $3,000 to $3,500. That is a much more palatable premium, especially if it frees up cash for other purposes.

When it is a business vehicle. If you are self-employed or operate a business, vehicle finance often comes with tax advantages. Interest repayments and depreciation can be deductible expenses under ATO rules. A chattel mortgage or novated lease structure can make the after-tax cost of borrowing significantly cheaper. Always speak to a tax professional about your specific situation, as the rules around vehicle deductions are detailed and depend on how you use the car.

The True Cost Comparison: A Real-World Scenario

You want to buy a $35,000 car. You have $35,000 in savings.

Option A — Pay outright. You transfer $35,000, buy the car, and own it immediately. Total cost: $35,000.

Option B — Put $5,000 down, take a 5-year loan at 8.5%. You borrow $30,000. Monthly repayment: $617. Total repaid: $37,020. The remaining $30,000 stays in a high-interest savings account at 5.5% for five years. That $30,000 grows to approximately $39,200 over five years. Net position: $39,200 minus $7,020 in interest paid — you are marginally better off financially by keeping your savings and financing the car, assuming the savings rate stays above the loan cost differential.

This exercise shows that the "always pay cash" rule is too simplistic. The right answer depends on your interest rate, your investment return, your tax position, and your personal risk tolerance. Use CalcPhi's Car Loan Calculator to work out your exact repayments and total interest, then plug that figure into the Compound Interest Calculator to see what your cash could have earned instead.

When Borrowing for a Car Is a Bad Idea

Despite the scenarios above, there are clear situations where a car loan will hurt you financially.

Taking a loan on a car you cannot comfortably afford is the most common mistake. Stretching to a seven-year loan on a $60,000 vehicle because the monthly repayment looks manageable is a trap. Over seven years at 9%, you pay more than $21,000 in interest. And cars depreciate — often 15–20% in the first year alone. By year three, you could owe more on the loan than the car is worth, a situation known as being "underwater" on the loan.

Taking a high-rate personal loan or using a dealership's in-house finance without comparing rates is another common error. Dealer finance is often significantly more expensive than what a bank or credit union would offer. Always shop around and compare the comparison rate before signing anything.

Finally, borrowing to buy a depreciating asset when you have no emergency fund in place adds financial fragility. If you lose your income or face an unexpected expense, that fixed monthly car repayment becomes a source of real stress. Your emergency fund should be intact before you add any new fixed debt obligation.

New Car vs Used Car: Does It Change the Borrowing Decision?

Yes. Used vehicles often attract higher interest rates from lenders — typically 1 to 3 percentage points higher than rates for new cars — because they carry more risk. They are also harder to insure for the full loan value if something goes wrong.

If you are buying a second-hand car for $15,000 to $20,000, it is often easier to save up and pay outright, given the smaller amount involved and the higher borrowing cost. For newer vehicles above $30,000, the loan versus cash analysis becomes worth doing properly.

Smart Borrowing Habits if You Do Take a Car Loan

If you decide a car loan is the right move, there are several ways to reduce the total cost. Put down the largest deposit you can comfortably manage — even adding $2,000 to $3,000 to your deposit meaningfully reduces total interest paid. Opt for the shortest repayment term your monthly cash flow allows — three years rather than five saves thousands. Make extra repayments when you can, if your loan allows it without penalty. And always compare at least three lenders before committing — use CalcPhi's Personal Loan Calculator to see how different rates and terms affect your total repayment.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • Is it better to get a car loan or pay cash in Australia?

    It depends on your interest rate, what your cash would otherwise earn, and your personal cash flow needs. If your car loan rate is lower than your investment return, keeping cash invested while financing the car can make mathematical sense. If you have no savings or investments, paying cash avoids interest entirely and is usually the simpler and safer choice.

  • What is the average car loan interest rate in Australia in 2026?

    Secured car loan rates for new vehicles in Australia currently range from approximately 7% to 10% per year, depending on the lender, your credit history, and the age of the vehicle. Manufacturer-backed promotional deals can sometimes offer lower rates. Always compare the comparison rate, not just the headline rate, to understand the true cost.

  • How much deposit should I put on a car loan?

    There is no fixed rule, but a deposit of 10% to 20% of the vehicle's drive-away price significantly reduces your loan amount and total interest paid. It also reduces the risk of being underwater on the loan, where you owe more than the car is worth due to depreciation.

  • Does paying cash for a car help you negotiate a better price?

    Often, yes. Cash buyers remove the dealer's opportunity to earn a finance margin, which can make them more willing to reduce the drive-away price. However, some dealers may still prefer finance customers due to incentive structures. Always negotiate the price before revealing your payment method.

  • Can I claim car loan interest as a tax deduction in Australia?

    Generally, no — not for a personal vehicle. However, if the vehicle is used for work or business purposes, you may be able to claim a portion of interest payments as a deduction under ATO rules. Self-employed individuals and business owners should speak with a registered tax agent to understand what applies to their situation.

  • What happens if I pay off my car loan early in Australia?

    Most lenders allow early repayment. However, some charge early exit fees or break costs, particularly on fixed-rate car loans. Always check your loan contract for early repayment terms before making extra payments or paying the loan out entirely.
